extracted.intended_audience: Authors and methodologists preparing Cochrane Overviews of Reviews (overview/umbrella review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical methodological and reporting guidance for planning, conducting, analysing, reporting, and updating Cochrane Overviews of Reviews (reviews of systematic reviews) addressing healthcare intervention questions. Focuses on inclusion criteria, searching, overlap management, data extraction, risk of bias, synthesis, GRADE, reporting, and updating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Cochrane Overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane Overviews of Reviews use explicit and systematic methods to search for and identify multiple systematic reviews on related research questions in the same topic area for the purpose of extracting and analysing their results across important outcomes. The unit of searching, inclusion and data analysis is the systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically conducted to answer questions about healthcare interventions; can include Cochrane and non-Cochrane systematic reviews; target audience includes healthcare decision makers (clinicians, policy makers, patients, funders). See V.2.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required components of a Cochrane Overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Overviews should contain five components: (1) a clearly formulated objective designed to answer a specific research question (typically about an intervention); (2) an intention to search for and include only systematic reviews; (3) explicit and reproducible methods to identify multiple systematic reviews and assess their quality/risk of bias; (4) intention to collect, analyse and present descriptive characteristics, risk of bias of primary studies, quantitative outcome data, and certainty of evidence (GRADE) for pre-defined important outcomes; (5) discussion relating findings to objectives including summary, completeness/applicability, quality, potential biases, and agreements/disagreements with other studies/reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components are modified from Pollock et al (2016). See V.2.2 for additional detail; all methods should be prespecified in a protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of research questions suitable for Overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Overviews can summarize evidence from two or more systematic reviews that: (a) examine different interventions for the same condition/population; (b) address different approaches to applying the same intervention for the same condition/population; (c) examine the same intervention for different conditions/populations; (d) address adverse effects of an intervention; (e) examine same intervention/same condition where different outcomes/time points are addressed in different reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overviews are often broader in scope than individual SRs. Authors may restrict attention to subsets of evidence (e.g. children only) but must justify restrictions and avoid inappropriate inferences (see V.2.3 and Table V.2.a).

rubrics_metrics.name: When not to conduct an Overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Overviews do not aim to: repeat/update searches or eligibility assessment of included SRs; conduct a study-level search for primary studies not included in any SR; conduct a new systematic review within the Overview; use SRs as a starting point to locate primary studies for extraction/analysis (this would be a systematic review); include narrative reviews/textbook chapters/guidelines that do not meet a pre-defined SR definition; extract only conclusions rather than actual outcome data; present detailed outcome data for primary studies not included in an included SR; or conduct network meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If primary-study searching or extraction is required, authors should instead conduct (or update) a systematic review of primary studies. See V.3.1 and V.3.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding indirect informal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Overviews should rarely be used to draw inferences about the comparative effectiveness of multiple interventions by informally comparing results across different SRs; authors should discourage or avoid indirect informal comparisons across SRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully worded research questions (e.g. 'Which interventions are effective?' not 'Which is best?'), interpret results appropriately, and provide clear explanations of dangers of informal indirect comparisons in text, tables, and figures. Indirect comparisons are discouraged because the transitivity assumption cannot usually be assessed using only information in SRs. See V.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the research question precisely (PICO & scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overview research questions should be specific, focused, and well-defined, including clear descriptions of populations, interventions, comparators, outcome measures, time periods, and settings. For Overviews examining different interventions, primary objective can be framed as: 'To summarize systematic reviews that assess the effects of [interventions] for [health problem] for/in [people, disease, setting]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Overviews are broad, consider restricting scope if heterogeneity across SR questions is substantial; any restrictions need adequate justification and should consider the decision-maker perspective. Document post-hoc modifications with rationale to avoid bias. See V.4.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop explicit inclusion criteria for systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion criteria should describe all relevant characteristics (populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes, time periods, settings) and specify the study design of interest as 'systematic review'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overview authors must specify operational criteria for what constitutes a 'systematic review' (e.g. explicit reproducible methods, comprehensive search, validity assessment). Non-Cochrane publications vary in labeling; pre-established criteria should guide inclusion decisions. See V.4.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to include variable study designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must consider whether to include SRs of randomized trials only, or SRs that include other designs (observational studies). Current guidance does not recommend combining randomized and observational data; if analyses mix designs, data must be presented/analysed separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If SRs present mixed designs, authors should ensure data are separable by design to allow separate analysis. See V.4.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for and manage overlapping systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate groups of SRs that examine the same intervention and include some of the same primary studies; consider in advance whether and how to include these overlapping reviews because they can introduce double-counting of primary study data and add complexity to all Overview stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate approaches vary by Overview purpose and analysis method — options include: include only Cochrane reviews; include all SRs and avoid double-counting by extracting each primary study's data only once; include all SRs regardless (but document overlap and limitations); include non-overlapping SRs and prioritize one SR per overlapping group (Cochrane, most recent, highest quality, most relevant, or most comprehensive). Use decision tool in Figure V.4.a and assess primary study overlap (see V.4.4 and V.4.7). Authors should operationalize prioritization criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and document primary study overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree of overlap of primary studies across included SRs (e.g. matrix/CCA) and document the extent of overlap and how it was handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlapping SRs may lead to double-counting outcome data and biased results. Choose methods to avoid double-counting if including overlapping SRs; if unable, provide methodological justification, quantify overlap, and discuss limitations. See V.4.7 and V.4.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision framework for inclusion of Cochrane vs non-Cochrane SRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a decision process to determine whether to include only Cochrane reviews (to reduce duplication and because they may be up-to-date/higher quality), or to search for and include non-Cochrane SRs when Cochrane coverage is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Cochrane reviews appear comprehensive, including only them may avoid overlap issues; otherwise search for non-Cochrane SRs (MEDLINE, Embase, Epistemonikos, KSR Evidence, regional databases). Reassess overlap and comprehensiveness after searching. See Decision points 1–4 in V.4.4 and V.4.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive and reproducible search for systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a literature search that is comprehensive and reproducible for identifying relevant systematic reviews; if including non-Cochrane SRs, search additional databases and SR repositories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEDLINE/PubMed and Embase index most SRs; consider regional/subject databases (LILACS, CINAHL, PsycINFO) and repositories (Epistemonikos, KSR Evidence). Use SR-specific terms and validated SR search filters; restrict searches to capture SRs while minimizing non-SR records. Document search strategies in protocol and supplementary materials. See V.4.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use validated search filters and SR-specific terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict searches to capture systematic reviews using search terms/MeSH headings specific to the SR design (e.g. 'systematic review', 'meta-analysis') and validated SR search filters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many databases index a wide variety of designs; authors should attempt to minimize capture of non-systematic publications. A list of validated search filters is provided in the chapter. See V.4.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening, selection, data extraction and quality assessment by independent reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is highly desirable that screening and inclusion, methodological quality/risk of bias assessments, and data extraction be conducted independently by two reviewers, with a process for resolving discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns with current Cochrane expectations for reviews of interventions. All methods should be pre-specified in the protocol. See V.4 and Table V.4.a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prespecify methods in a protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: All methods for conducting the Overview (eligibility criteria, searching, selection, data collection, quality assessment, analysis, management of overlap) should be considered in advance and detailed in a protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocol sections for Overviews are listed in Box V.5.a (title, background, objectives, methods including criteria for selecting reviews, search methods, data collection and analysis, quality of included reviews, risk of bias of primary studies, quality of evidence; additional info: declarations, registration, data/code). Document any post-hoc modifications with rationale. See V.4 and Box V.5.a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess methodological quality / risk of bias of included systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and report the methodological quality/risk of bias of included systematic reviews (i.e. critical appraisal of review conduct and reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the quality/risk of bias of included SRs and consider using established tools (e.g. AMSTAR/AMSTAR2, ROBIS). Use these assessments to inform inclusion decisions or sensitivity analyses (see V.4.9 and references to AMSTAR/ROBIS guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and present risk of bias of primary studies within included SRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and present data on risk of bias (or methodological quality) of the primary studies contained within included systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If SRs report risk of bias assessments of their included primary studies, extract and present those; if not, consider whether to conduct own assessments (resource-intensive). Report how primary-study bias information was handled and its implications for synthesis. See V.4.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and present descriptive characteristics of included SRs and their primary studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract and report descriptive characteristics of included systematic reviews (and where possible characteristics of their primary studies), such as populations, interventions/comparators, outcomes, time points, settings, dates, and included primary studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present characteristics in tables and supplementary materials (e.g. 'Characteristics of included reviews', 'Characteristics of excluded reviews', 'Characteristics of reviews awaiting assessment', 'Characteristics of ongoing reviews'). See V.4.11 and Box V.5.b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting, analysing and presenting quantitative outcome data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect quantitative outcome data as reported in included SRs (narratively reported study-level data and/or meta-analysed data). Overviews may present outcome data exactly as they appear in included SRs or re-analyse SR outcome data differently from the included analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-analysing, take care to avoid double-counting primary-study data (see overlap guidance). Consider whether data reported in SRs are sufficient for desired analyses; if not, a primary-study review may be preferable. Present results in tables/figures and consider summary of findings tables. See V.4.12 and Table V.4.c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and report certainty of evidence using GRADE
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the GRADE tool to assess and report the certainty of evidence for each pre-defined, clinically important outcome in the Overview. If possible, extract and report GRADE assessments presented in included SRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: some SRs may not contain GRADE, may use other tools, or present aggregated assessments. If Overviews re-extract/re-analyse outcome data, existing GRADE assessments may not be relevant and the Overview authors may need to conduct GRADE assessments themselves using reported information. See V.4.13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and reporting unique requirements for Overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow reporting guidance similar to Cochrane reviews but with unique requirements: titles should contain the phrase 'an Overview of Reviews'; titles should state whether Cochrane reviews and/or non-Cochrane SRs are included; section headings should refer to 'reviews' not 'studies'; include separate subheadings for methodological quality of included SRs and of their underlying primary studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections of protocol and review are listed in Box V.5.a and Box V.5.b. Include summary of findings tables, plain language summary, and discuss limitations specific to Overviews (coverage of SRs, missing data, bias introduced at both review and overview levels). See V.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of findings (SoF) tables for Overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare 'Summary of findings' tables tailored to Overviews that present outcomes, interventions/comparators, illustrative comparative risks (95% CI), relative effect (95% CI), number of participants (studies), and certainty of the evidence (GRADE), with comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template provided in Table V.4.c. Multiple intervention-comparator rows may be needed for different SRs; ensure presentation avoids encouraging informal indirect comparisons. See V.4.12 and Table V.4.c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting limitations and potential biases specific to Overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In Discussion, report unique limitations: whether all relevant SRs were identified/included, gaps in coverage of existing SRs, whether all relevant data could be obtained, implications of missing data, and whether methods at both SR and Overview levels could have introduced bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also discuss agreements/disagreements with other studies/reviews, overall completeness/applicability of evidence, and implications for practice/research. See V.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating Overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular updating of Cochrane Overviews is important and follows the same process as updating Cochrane reviews of interventions; small updates may suffice, but new eligible SRs or major changes in included Cochrane reviews may require extensive revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider update frequency, re-running searches, reassessing inclusion as new SRs appear, and documenting update history. See V.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not extract only conclusions from included SRs; extract outcome data
rubrics_metrics.description: Overview authors should not extract and present just the conclusions of included SRs; actual outcome data (narratively reported study-level data and/or meta-analysed data) should be extracted and analysed, and authors are encouraged to interpret these outcome data themselves in light of the Overview’s questions/objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracting only conclusions is an anti-pattern because conclusions may be inconsistently derived, incomplete, or not aligned with the Overview question. See V.3.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize criteria for prioritizing among overlapping SRs
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing among overlapping reviews (e.g. including only one review from a group), operationalize what 'most recent', 'highest quality', 'most relevant', or 'most comprehensive' mean and apply pre-specified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritization is a trade-off between comprehensiveness and avoiding double-counting; document the prioritization criteria and rationale. See V.4.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting methods, decisions and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: All inclusion decisions, handling of overlap, search strategies, screening, extraction, quality assessments, and any post-hoc modifications must be documented with rationale in the protocol and final report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is required so readers can assess potential biases introduced by overview-level decisions (e.g. exclusion of poorly conducted SRs based on quality assessments). Provide supplementary materials (search strategies, characteristics of included/excluded reviews, data package). See V.4, V.5 and Boxes V.5.a/b.
